clue.text: Peter (Potter) is no match for Tiger

definitions.meaning: Beatrix Potter's Peter, the mischievous bunny of her children's tales
a hopeless player, a duffer at a game, is no match for a champion such as a golfer nicknamed Tiger

explanation.definitionFit: Beatrix Potter's Peter is that animal by species, and a weak, unskilled player of a game is also called by its name in British sporting slang.

clue.text: Blue as Britannia's 25

parts.note: entry 25 gives the word for the sea; the song Rule, Britannia! begins with Britain rising 'from out the — main', the blank being a sky-blue colour word

explanation.walkthrough: Rule, Britannia! is a patriotic British song whose first verse has Britain arising 'from out the azure main'; 25 is the cross-reference to the answer for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in the song's line names a bright sky-blue colour, so it is a shade of blue.

clue.text: Say, what b-- officiousness ?

parts.note: the b-word with its letters blanked is the name of the pompous parish beadle of Oliver Twist, and the clue asks what to call his brand of officiousness

explanation.walkthrough: Mr Bumble is the self-important beadle (a minor parish official) in Dickens's Oliver Twist; the blank after 'b' asks the solver to supply his name, and the suffix -dom turns it into a word for petty official arrogance.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the fussy self-importance of minor officials, after a pompous Dickens beadle, which is officiousness in its purest form.

clue.text: Uncle's carelessly rapturous opponent

annotationWithheld.why: Uncle's carelessly rapturous opponent (6): 'carelessly rapturous' alludes to Browning's thrush with its 'first fine careless rapture', but no source found explains whose 'opponent' it is or what 'Uncle's' refers to.

clue.text: All the runners have time for this military occasion

parts.note: the field is everyone running in a race
a day is a period of time

explanation.surface: Every competitor in a race makes time to watch a parade.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally the phrase meant a day of military manoeuvres or a review of troops, before it came to mean any great opportunity.

clue.text: Peter, in a church-building context, discovered at one to be overweight

parts.note: to have discovered something is to have found it
the Roman numeral for one is I
on can mean over, as a book on the table
a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: Someone digging around a church learns that Peter carries too much weight.
explanation.walkthrough: Christ called Peter the rock on which he would build his church, so in that context Peter is its first, supporting block. A STONE is a British unit of weight (14 lb); 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter is the rock on which the Church was built, the first block laid beneath it, as a ceremonial base block is for a building.

clue.text: The golden sovereign of Manoa

parts.note: Spanish legend told of a king of the fabled city of Manoa who was covered in gold dust, 'the gilded one'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Golden sovereign' suggests the British gold coin, but here it is a ruler: the gilded king of the mythical South American city of Manoa sought by conquistadors.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish phrase means 'the gilded one', first the gold-dusted king of the legend, later the legendary city of gold itself.

clue.text: Spud, or what to do with it

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to spud is to dig out with a small spade
a spud is also a potato, which you lift out of the ground at harvest

explanation.definitionFit: To spud is to excavate with a narrow spade, and the potato itself must be lifted from the soil to be harvested.

clue.text: Fixed price aids paper, oddly enough

indicators.note: oddly says these letters are put together in a strange order to form a new word

explanation.surface: Selling paper for a set sum seems a strange way to help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed price' looks like a noun phrase, but it is a verb with its object: to have put a price on something. 'oddly enough' rearranges AIDS PAPER.
explanation.definitionFit: Valuing something means setting what it is worth, so a valuer has put a figure on it.

clue.text: Such a bind round the Equator, dressing for dinner !

definitions.text: Such a bind round the Equator, dressing for dinner !

parts.words: Such a bind round the Equator, dressing for dinner !
parts.note: the Equator is the body's waistline, and the bind is a sash worn round it with evening dress

explanation.walkthrough: The 'Equator' is the waist, and a 'bind' is a band tied round it: the pleated sash worn with a dinner jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: This pleated sash is wrapped round the waist as part of formal evening wear.

clue.text: Doctor without a direction to " Open wide "

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the doctor's letters go round the a

parts.note: GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor
E is east, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A dentist's instruction to open wide, given without a doctor present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' means 'outside' here, putting GP round A to make GAP, then E (east) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To open the mouth wide is to stare or yawn open-mouthed.

clue.text: Read about the oddest lies made to come true

indicators.note: about means the word read goes round the other letters
the oddest arrangement of these letters is a new order of them

explanation.surface: Someone discovers that the strangest lies they read have come true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddest' turns LIES into LISE, and 'about' puts READ round it: REA + LISE + D.
explanation.definitionFit: To realise a plan or dream is to make it real, bringing it into actual existence.

clue.text: No new programme about — fuel

parts.note: re means about or concerning
peat is dug and burned as fuel

explanation.surface: A complaint that there is no fresh programme about fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: A rerun broadcast is a programme shown again, not a new one.

clue.text: Players said to be not allowed

indicators.note: said signals a word that sounds like the one meant

parts.note: something not allowed is banned

explanation.surface: Some players are rumoured to have been banned.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of musicians who perform together is a musical ensemble.

clue.text: Ease with which everyone gets over the Paris season by way of entering it

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over, above, the rest

parts.note: all means everyone

indicators.note: entering means one piece goes inside the other, here into the season

parts.note: été is French for summer, a season in Paris
via means by way of

explanation.surface: Everyone eases through the Paris season by travelling into it.
explanation.walkthrough: ÉTÉ is French for summer; 'entering it' puts VIA inside it to make EVIATE, and 'gets over' puts ALL above that in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve pain or distress is to lessen it, making it lighter to bear.

clue.text: Such a sea has no foreshore

definitions.text: Such a sea has no foreshore

parts.words: Such a sea has no foreshore
parts.note: the foreshore is the strip between high and low water, which only exists where the water rises and falls

explanation.walkthrough: The foreshore is the shore between the high- and low-water marks, so a sea such as the Mediterranean, with almost no rise and fall, has none.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea without rise and fall of its water has no intertidal strip for a foreshore.

clue.text: Ways to avoid water, back on parts of course

indicators.note: back means the word for water is read from right to left

parts.note: a pool is a body of water
a golf course is divided into holes

explanation.surface: Walkers on a golf course find ways round the water hazards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns POOL into LOOP; 'on' sets it above HOLES in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaps in a rule that let someone escape its effect are means of evasion.

clue.text: What ho ! Trouble over the Navy plant ?

indicators.note: trouble means the letters are stirred up into a new order

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A cheery greeting before a row about a factory belonging to the Navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' scrambles WHAT HO into HAWTHO; 'over' sets it above RN, the Royal Navy, in the down entry. 'Plant' looks like a factory but is a shrub.
explanation.definitionFit: This thorny shrub of English hedgerows, the may, is a flowering plant.

clue.text: Flower from a pencil ?

definitions.meaning: a blue-flowered climbing shrub, Cape leadwort, is a garden flower
the 'lead' of a pencil is in fact graphite, once called black lead

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the leadwort shrub with its pale blue blooms and the graphite core of a pencil.

clue.text: Chances are the large size is about twopence

indicators.note: is about means one piece goes round the other

parts.note: OS is short for outsize, the large size in clothes
d was the symbol for an old penny, so two pence is two of them

explanation.surface: The odds are that the large size costs about twopence.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British pennies were written d, so twopence is DD; 'is about' puts OS (outsize) round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Betting chances are expressed as ratios of probability, the likelihood of something happening.

clue.text: Puppies make a mess !

definitions.meaning: a set of young born to a bitch at one birth

explanation.definitionFit: One word names a brood of newborn animals born together and also the act of scattering rubbish untidily.

clue.text: Wader's bill gets involved with something slithy

definitions.note: the 's stands for is: the wader is what the rest makes

indicators.note: involved means tangled together, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: a/c is short for account, a bill
Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky has 'slithy toves', so a tove is something slithy

explanation.surface: A wading bird's beak gets tangled up with something slimy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' suggests a beak, but it is AC (account); 'gets involved with' mixes AC with TOVE, from the 'slithy toves' of Carroll's nonsense poem Jabberwocky.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-legged black-and-white bird with an upturned bill feeds in shallow water, a wading bird.

clue.text: Jargon gets round to poetry

parts.note: cant is the jargon of a particular group
the letter O is round

explanation.surface: Specialist jargon finds its way into verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A division of a long poem is a section of poetry.

clue.text: Youth out for scalps ?

parts.note: scalps suggests a warrior taking trophies, but the young man's own scalp is laid bare by a crew cut

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a young warrior hunting scalps; in fact the youth shows off his own scalp, shaved to the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A young man with a close-shaven head belongs to a youth subculture named after that bare scalp.

clue.text: A strange urge this to make holes

indicators.note: strange means the letters are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A peculiar compulsion to bore holes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges URGE into UGER after A. The definition is 'this to make holes', a tool for the job.
explanation.definitionFit: A boring tool with a spiral bit is used for drilling into wood or ground.

clue.text: Island without a single chief

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the island goes round the single

parts.note: Man is the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea
I is the Roman numeral for one, a single

explanation.surface: An island lacking a single leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means 'outside': MAN (the Isle of Man) round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Principal or most important, as in the major road or event, means chief.

clue.text: The " O stop ! " science

parts.note: the cry 'O stop!' can be put as 'O, don't!', and a science is an -ology

explanation.walkthrough: 'O stop!' is 'O, don't!', which run together begins the word, and the study of teeth also deals in fillings, once called stoppings.
explanation.definitionFit: The study of teeth and their diseases is the dental science.

clue.text: Accuse the numskull who holds one back

indicators.note: holds means the dunce goes round the other piece

parts.note: a dunce is a numskull, a slow learner

indicators.note: back means the word one is written right to left

explanation.surface: Someone accuses the fool who holds one person back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ONE into ENO, and 'who holds' puts DUNCE round it.
explanation.definitionFit: To condemn someone publicly or inform against them is to accuse them.

clue.text: In Holiday Haunts was Thule the last one ?

definitions.text: In Holiday Haunts was Thule the last one ?

parts.words: In Holiday Haunts was Thule the last one ?
parts.note: Holiday Haunts was a railway guide to holiday towns; Ultima Thule was the farthest place of the ancient world, so it would be the final option, a 'last' place to go

explanation.walkthrough: Holiday Haunts was a British railway guidebook to seaside towns; Ultima Thule was the Romans' edge of the world, so in such a guide it would be the 'last' holiday place, playing on the phrase for a final option.
explanation.definitionFit: A holiday town is a place people go for leisure, and the phrase 'last ...' means a final expedient.
